subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Moroccan Mint Tea: Atay
description: A short lesson to help you apply Moroccan Mint Tea: Atay.

hook.text: Moroccan mint tea (atay) is gunpowder green tea with fresh spearmint and generous sugar. Pouring is a performance.

buildup.text: Tea is poured from high—sometimes a meter above the glass—to create a frothy head and mix the sugar evenly.

discovery.text: The pour's height also cools the tea slightly and aerates it, improving both texture and aroma.

twist.text: Three glasses are customary: the first gentle like life, the second strong like love, the third bitter like death.

climax.text: Refusing a glass of atay in Morocco is a serious social offense. Tea is hospitality made liquid.

punchline.text: High pour, sweet glass, three rounds of hospitality. That's Morocco.

quiz.question: Why is Moroccan mint tea poured from a great height?
options: To cool, aerate, and mix sugar while creating a frothy head

details.summary: Moroccan mint tea, or atay, is a blend of Chinese gunpowder green tea and fresh spearmint leaves, sweetened generously with sugar. It is poured from height to create a frothy top. Serving tea is an essential act of hospitality in Morocco, and refusing it is considered deeply impolite.
details.whyItMatters: Moroccan mint tea shows how a Chinese export was transformed into a distinctly North African tradition. It is the country's most important symbol of hospitality.
takeaways: Atay combines gunpowder green tea with fresh spearmint
It is poured from height to create a frothy head
Serving and accepting tea is a fundamental act of hospitality

faq.question: Why is the tea poured from such a height?
faq.answer: Pouring from height aerates the tea, creating froth on top and cooling it slightly. It also mixes the sugar more thoroughly. The dramatic pour is a practiced skill that adds theatricality to the serving ritual. A good pour is a source of pride for the host.

faq.question: How many glasses of Moroccan tea are traditionally served?
faq.answer: Traditionally three glasses are served. A Moroccan proverb describes them: the first glass is gentle as life, the second is strong as love, the third is bitter as death. Leaving before the third glass is considered rude. The progression reflects deepening friendship between host and guest.
